editorNote: The personal-computer boom is becoming a contest over standards, shelves, and survival. IBM sets the pace, portable makers feel the strain, and ambitious games make home machines worlds of their own.
morningLine: IBM compatibility, portable-computer turmoil, and Ultima III define the week.

lead.headline: IBM's PC Standard Tightens Its Grip
lead.dek: The two-year-old IBM PC has taken the sales lead, inspired a compatible-machine industry, and left once-hot independents scrambling for position.
body: NEW YORK — The personal-computer trade has rarely moved so quickly from open field to established order. TIME reports this week that IBM's Personal Computer, introduced only in August 1981, now accounts for 26 percent of unit sales and has displaced Apple from first place.

The market around it is expanding at a dizzying rate. More than 200 American manufacturers are competing, twice the number of two years ago, while 1983 sales are forecast at seven million machines. Roughly 20 companies already offer IBM-compatible computers, evidence that buyers increasingly prize access to the software and dealers gathered around one standard.

That concentration is exacting a price. Osborne cut its pioneering Osborne 1 from $1,795 to $1,295 after advance word of the Executive slowed current sales. Vector Graphic turned a 1981 profit into a 1982 loss and has laid off a quarter of its workforce; Victor Technologies reported an $11 million second-quarter loss and eliminated 350 jobs.

There are winners as well as casualties. Kaypro founder Andrew Kay has enjoyed an estimated $245 million paper gain after his company's stock offering. Yet the lesson from showroom to boardroom is the same: technical novelty is no longer enough. Compatibility, software, distribution, and the ability to deliver the next model without sinking the present one now determine who remains in the race.

stories.headline: Ultima III Makes the Quest a Team Affair
stories.dek: Origin's Exodus expands the computer role-playing form with four adventurers, tactical battles, and a richly furnished box.
body: A new fantasy epic is giving Apple II owners an unusually ambitious journey. Richard Garriott's Ultima III: Exodus replaces the lone adventurer of earlier games with a party of four characters, each chosen and developed to contribute different skills.

Combat now moves to separate tactical screens, turning encounters into contests of position as well as preparation. The change gives the party structure real purpose and pushes the computer role-playing game toward a more deliberate blend of exploration, statistics, and battlefield command.

Origin Systems also treats the package as part of the adventure. A cloth map and extensive materials make Exodus feel less like a bare disk and more like a boxed world, a standard other computer-game publishers will find difficult to ignore.

stories.headline: Portable Computers Crowd the Departure Gate
stories.dek: BYTE surveys a growing field of luggables as Kaypro prospers and Osborne struggles through a painful model change.
body: Portable computing has grown from curiosity into a category crowded with choices. BYTE's September cover package examines CP/M luggables including the Osborne 1, Kaypro II, Zorba, and Pied Piper I, machines that promise a familiar office environment in a case that can travel.

The business fortunes behind those handles differ sharply. TIME estimates a $245 million paper gain for Kaypro founder Andrew Kay after the company's offering, while Osborne canceled its planned offering amid slowing sales and trouble bridging the Osborne 1 to its announced Executive.

These are transportable rather than effortless companions: displays are small, cases are heavy, and wall power remains essential. Still, bundling a screen, drives, and useful software in one enclosure is changing what buyers expect a complete computer to be.

stories.headline: Cellular Service Moves Toward the Marketplace
stories.dek: Ameritech forms a subsidiary to offer cellular mobile telephone service in the Midwest.
body: CHICAGO — Ameritech announced on September 1 that it has organized a subsidiary to offer mobile telephone service using cellular technology. The parent of five Midwestern Bell companies describes the unit as the first of its kind organized for the new service.

Cellular systems divide a territory into small radio areas and reuse frequencies as callers move between them, offering a path beyond the limited capacity of conventional mobile telephone networks. The announcement arrives just ahead of commercial cellular service expected in Chicago.

The early handsets and car installations will be costly, and coverage will begin in selected cities. Even so, the organizational step signals that a long-demonstrated technology is becoming a consumer communications business.
